Driving as Side TaskExploring Intuitive Input Modalities for Multitasking in Automated VehiclesHenrik Detjenhenrik.detjen@hs-ruhrwest.deUniv. of Appl. Sciences Ruhr WestBottrop, GermanyStefan Geislerstefan.geisler@hs-ruhrwest.deUniv. of Appl. Sciences Ruhr WestBottrop, GermanyStefan Schneegassstefan.schneegass@uni-due.deUniversity of Duisburg-EssenEssen, GermanyABSTRACTThrough vehicle automation, the human is more and more ableto execute non-driving-related activities (NDRAs). However, con-trol interfaces are still needed to allow human intervention andfoster a sense of control. This paper presents a driving simulatorexperiment (N = 20) with five likely NDRAs (being idle, eating,smartphone use, conversation, listen to music) where participantsfreely intervened in the driving process, using either touch, voice,or mid-air gesture interaction. We found that NDRAs determineinput modality choices. Generally, participants tended to avoid themodalities demanded by the NDRAs, e.g., voice interaction becomesless frequent while listening to music. Contrary, touch interactionincreased during smartphone use, indicating that users tend to stickto a known interaction style during high multitasking workload.Overall, we recommend designing future vehicle interiors and inter-faces that rely on multimodal interfaces to account for the diversityof situations and activities while driving automated.CCS CONCEPTS• Human-centered computing → Human computer interac-tion (HCI); User studies; Interaction techniques.KEYWORDSAutomated Vehicles, Non-Driving-Related Activities, Driving-RelatedActivities, Maneuver-based Interventions, Control, Multitasking,Multimodal Interaction, Touch, Voice, Mid-Air Gestures.ACM Reference Format:Henrik Detjen, Stefan Geisler, and Stefan Schneegass. 2021. Driving as SideTask: Exploring Intuitive Input Modalities for Multitasking in AutomatedVehicles. Traditionally thedriver is responsible for the driving task. Publication rights licensed to ACM.ACM ISBN 978-1-4503-8095-9/21/05. . . $15.00https://doi.org/10.1145/3411763.3451803Reaching certain degrees of automation (cf., SAE level 3–5 [22]),the system can complete the driving task itself, at least for a cer-tain time, depending on the level. From then on, the human driverbecomes the passenger (e.g., from entering until exiting the high-way) and is free to engage in non-driving-related activities (abbr.:NDRAs): one can do work, entertainment, or social activities duringtravel. Nevertheless, even in autonomous driving phases, human-vehicle interaction is still necessary to provide mechanisms to thehuman driver to intervene in the driving task, e.g., to adapt driv-ing parameters, take cooperative maneuvers, or foster a sense ofcontrol. The NDRAs highly influence the context of such driving-related activities (abbr.: DRAs). When the occupants want to in-tervene in the driving process, they must shift their attention tothe new task, and the current activity must be interrupted. Inter-ference between NDRA and DRA because of similar requirementsfor spatial/verbal cognitive resources (cf. [25]), might lead to per-formance breakdowns. Thus, it is crucial to understand the inter-play between NDRA and DRAs in automated vehicles. While thedefinition [19], prediction [5, 12, 13, 18], and automated recogni-tion [17] of NDRAs, as well as their influence on take-over requestperformance [6, 10, 15, 20, 27] have been studied recently, theirinfluence in less critical multitasking scenarios is still unexplored.This paper therefore explores the influence of highly anticipatednon-driving-related activities (main task) on the driver/passenger’smodality choices when intervening in the driving process (sidetask) in a driving simulator experiment (N = 20). To interact in asubjectively natural and comfortable way, participants could freelychoose between touch, voice, and mid-air gesture modalities. Wewere interested in resulting patterns of interaction and possibledifferences in multitasking performance. Thereby, we hypothesizethat (1) NDRAs would influence the chosen input modalities forcontrol interventions, and (2) the selected modality would be differ-ent from the modality used for the main task. Our study helps tounderstand better which interaction modalities are used naturally inthe context of different NDRAs. Further, it is a first step towards theactivity-optimized development of in-car HMIs for driving-relatedcontrol interventions in future automated cars.2 RELATED WORKIn the following, we distinguish DRAs from NDRAs and show howcontrol in automated cars will change. The growing automationwill lead to new activities, and new activities will change the userrequirements for in-car interfaces.2.1 Non-Driving-Related ActivitiesIn conventional cars, one can divide the driving task into threecategories (cf. Bubb [1]): 1) transportation-related tasks which are
Page 2
CHI ’21 Extended Abstracts, May 8–13, 2021, Yokohama, Japan Detjen, Geisler & Schneegassrequired to reach a destination (e.g., use the steering wheel), 2)transportation-related tasks which are optional to reach a par-ticular destination (e.g., use the windscreen wiper), and 3) non-transportation-related tasks (e.g., use media control).With the system’s growing responsibility for the primary andsecondary driving tasks through automation, the former driverbecomes more and more a passenger in automated cars, and ter-tiary tasks become more important than before. To simplify thecategorization of tasks in automated vehicles, we use the termsDriving-Related Activities or Tasks and Non-Driving-Related Activ-ities or Tasks as proposed by Pfleging & Schmidt [19]. ExpectedNDRAs are, for example [5, 12, 13, 18]: Watching out of the win-dow, talking to other passengers, using the smartphone, eating,listen to music/radio, taking a nap, knitting, or office work. Theseactivities require different physical and cognitive resources andinfluence the human vehicle user’s capabilities and preferences tocontrol the car.2.2 Control During Autonomous DrivingAn essential requirement of cooperative driving is directability [24].From a functional perspective, use cases where the human mightwant to intervene in an automated ride are, for example [23]: Influ-encing the route taken, adjusting the driving style of the vehicle(e.g., to accelerate more quickly at the traffic light), or overtakingof slow traffic before the highway exit. From a psychological per-spective, it is beneficial to provide a control interface possibility.Compared to being passive in autonomous driving, the possibilityto exercise control increases driving pleasure and attractiveness [9]and the acceptance of the system [16].Traditional controls (steering wheel and pedals) might not be thebest option because they require detailed awareness of the drivingsituation on the operational level, e.g., the exact steering angle fora DRA. A more comfortable way of controlling the car could bemaneuver-based or trajectory-based control [7] because operationalaspects of the driving task remain with the vehicle. We refer tothese concepts as Trajetory-based Interventions and Maneuver-basedInterventions (abbr.: MBI). Such cooperative concepts combine theadvantage of automated driving with user needs and requirements.Because these driving interventions are intentional actions of thedriver/passenger, interfaces for maneuver control commonly relyon explicit and fast interaction modalities, e.g., touch [8, 14], voice,or mid-air gestures [3, 4]. However, objective utility and subjec-tive perception of these interfaces are heavily dependent on theinteraction context and, thus, on the NDRAs.2.3 Multitasking and Multimodal InteractionDuring autonomous travel times, vehicle occupants are likely toperform NDRAs. When they are occupied with a particular NDRA,they spend physical and mental resources for that task, e.g., read-ing a book requires the physical effort to hold the book and themental effort to decode and understand the written letters – eyesand hands, as well as attention, are dedicated to this task. Controlinterventions potentially use the same and thus might interferewith these resources. Wickens [26] defines four dimensions of re-source sharing in multitasking settings: 1) processing dimension(perception, cognition, response), 2) codes of processing dimen-sion (spatial vs verbal), 3) modalities dimension (auditory vs visualperception), and 4) visual channels (focal vs ambient). The less amultitasking procedure occupies the same dimensions, the betterthe later performance.Roider et al. [21] found for input modality switches for sidetasks during driving, that transitions between interaction modali-ties can increase efficiency compared to unimodal conditions andthat switching modalities does not increase overall task comple-tion time. Further, their results indicate that distractions from themain task are determined by the used modality of the side task,not by transition processes. Once distraction from the main task(driving) is no longer the primary concern of interaction, the sys-tem should promote modality switches between tasks so that userscould benefit from individual modality’s efficiency and suitabilityfor a particular task. Thus, it might be useful to switch controlintervention modality during an NDRA, e.g., voice control wouldnot be the best choice while listening to music, and touch not thebest choice while using the smartphone.3 EXPERIMENTWe conducted a within-subject driving simulator experiment toexplore modality choices for control interventions in multitaskingscenarios. On a short test track, participants performed five possi-ble non-driving-related activities (counterbalanced order) duringwhich they intervened four times in the driving process. Each timethey could choose between either voice, touch, or mid-air gestures(resulting in 20 choices per participant or 80 choices per condition).Sample. We conducted the study at the University of Applied Sci-ences Ruhr West. Twenty computer science students (m = 17; f = 3)with an average age of 22.45 years (SD = 4.55; Min = 18; Max = 33)participated.Task A: Driving-Related Activity. We told participants that theywould ride a safe driving car (cf. driving phases during SAE level3–5) operating in a cooperative driving mode that requires their con-trol. We instructed participants to adhere to the following routineduring the rides, intervening in the autonomous driving process:A1) start the vehicle (start maneuver), A2) command the car to driveonto the motorway from the rest area (lane change maneuver), A3)control the vehicle to leave the highway at the next rest area (lanechange maneuver), and A4) park at a rest area (park maneuver).Participants were free to choose an interaction modality out ofvoice, touch, and mid-air gestures. We selected these modalitiesbecause they allow for direct interaction. For touch interaction, weused a maneuver-board interface on a touchpad (identical to [14]),and for voice and mid-air gesture interfaces, we used a user-definedcommand set (identical to [3]).Task B: Non-Driving-Related Activity. Based on studies on ex-pected NDRAs (cf. [5, 12, 18]), we discussed frequent activitiesconcerning their potential impact on driving-related interventions.Afterward, we selected five prototypical activities for our exper-iment that would involve participants in different ways. For theselected tasks, we gave participants the following instructions inaddition to Task A (cf. Table 1).Setup and Wizard of Oz.
